newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries rally on June employment report.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries rally on June employment report.

text.p: By Ellen Freilich
A June U.S. employment report that portrayed moderate jobs growth and a near absence of wage inflation sent U.S. bond and stock prices soaring on Thursday.
At midday, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was near its highest level of the day, up 1-11/32 to 100-8/32. Its 6.60 percent yield was the lowest for the bond since mid-February.
In the stock market, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 84.60 to 7880.20 after reaching an all-time high of 7896.26 earlier in the session.

Near the start of the trading session, the Labor Department reported that U.S. non-farm payrolls grew by 217,000 new jobs in June. Combined with May's revised payroll growth of 166,000 new jobs, the numbers offered a picture of moderate job growth in the second quarter.

A jump in the unemployment rate to 5.0 percent in June from 4.8 percent in May also comforted investors who spent some months worrying that a tight labor market would lead to upward pressure on wages and eventually to higher prices.
The hourly wage data in the employment report was also good news for inflation-wary bond investors.
The Labor Department said hourly wages rose 4 cents to $12.22 in June from $12.18 in May, bringing year-over-year wages gains to 3.5 percent, off a March peak of 4.1 percent.
Separately, Labor also reported that new claims for state unemployment insurance edged up to 337,000 in the week ended June 28 from 332,000 a week earlier.
"Everyone's being dragged into the market," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi. "Every account wants to get long."
Rupkey said it was irregular for the bond to "gap up" a point and then trend higher making new highs every half hour.

"That indicates that retail is involved," he said. "If these bonds come off 3/4 of a point next week, there will be people willing to buy," Rupkey said. "The (upward) trend has gone on too long. People are kicking themselves for not having bought earlier in the week. There's a lot of lamenting going on. People are unhappy that they missed it."
Lee Youngdahl, Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. bond analyst, said the June payroll data pointed to a modest rebound in economic growth in the third quarter but gave no evidence of inflation.
"The Fed is letting growth run a bit faster as long as inflation doesn't pick up," he said.
"This presents a benign equation for bonds and equities so money managers are reinvesting their cash," said Youngdahl.
Modest wage increases in May and June also alleviated concerns about upward pressure on wages, he said.
"Those concerns will linger since the economy is operating at a high rate but the numbers tell the story," he said.
Youngdahl said technicals would drive the market higher next week.
"The momentum players still want to buy dips and it looks like we'll take a shot at 6.50 percent or 6.55 percent (on the 30-year bond yield)," he said.
"Flows from domestic and foreign buyers were evident today and the momentum builds on itself," said Youngdahl. "There aren't many sellers around."
Before the market closes early at 1500 EDT/1900 GMT for the Independence Day holiday weekend, investors will get the minutes from the May 20 Federal Open Market Committee meeting.

"The expectation is that the committee went to a tightening bias at the May 20 meeting," said Rupkey "If that doesn't materialize, that will tell people that the Fed is less concerned about inflation. It would push off the timing of another rate hike even further down the road."
In afternoon trade, ten-year notes were up 24/32 to 102-10/32, yielding 6.31 percent. Five-year notes were 14/32 to 100-7/32 to yield 6.20 percent.
Three-month bill rates were down eight basis points to 5.01 percent. Six-month bill rates were down four basis point to 5.06 percent and year bill rates were down seven basis points to 5.26 percent.
Two-year notes were up 5/32, yielding 5.93 percent.
((--North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679))
